extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, mathematicians, and experimental scientists (readers of Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and methodological recommendations for constructing roots of cubic and biquadratic (third- and fourth-degree) equations by means of a given parabola and a circle, including reductions, choice of conventions, and geometric steps. Also includes experimental-design guidance for pneumatics, distillation, and magnetic-variation observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descartes' construction using one parabola and a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: How all equations that involve the third or fourth power of the unknown quantity may be constructed by means of any given parabola and a circle (Descartes' construction): when the second term is wanting reduce to canonical form and then use geometric operations (take specified segments on the parabola's axis and erect perpendiculars; describe a circle on a centre determined by those segments) so that intersections of the circle with the parabola give the true roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise recipe given: when the second term is absent reduce the equation to the form z^3 + pz - q = 0 (or the corresponding biquadratic form); take the given parabola whose latus rectum = a (or set a=1); set AC = 1/2 a and CD = p/2 (with sign conventions); erect DE = q/2 (with sign conventions) perpendicular to the axis; a circle described with centre E and radius AE (or adjusted radius for biquadratics) will intersect the parabola in as many points as the equation has true roots; dropping perpendiculars to the axis from those intersections yields the roots (affirmative on the right of the axis, negative on the left). The text gives multiple worked examples and figures and notes many sign/placement cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove the second term by substitution before geometric construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The second term (the x^2 term in biquadratic/cubic forms) should be eliminated by an appropriate substitution so the resulting equation fits Descartes' form and is amenable to the parabola+circle construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: substitute z = x + (appropriate quantity depending on the coefficient signs) to produce a new equation 'wanting the second term' and then apply Descartes' construction to that reduced equation. Several algebraic examples are worked through showing the correct half-coefficients to use in locating the geometric elements (centre and radius). The method clarifies Baker's and Schooten's rules by giving an explicit substitution-based reduction; follow the worked examples to determine the exact substitution in each sign-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place affirmative roots consistently on the right of the axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the convention of placing affirmative (positive) roots on the right side of the axis to avoid repeated cautions and sign-confusion in constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly prefers always to have the affirmative roots on the right to simplify the method and 'avoid the confusion necessarily arising from a great number of cautions'. When performing constructions, set off positive-signed members towards the left hand of the axis and negative toward the right (or vice versa as prescribed) so that the final perpendiculars give affirmative roots on the chosen side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust the circle's radius for biquadratic equations by adding/subtracting ar
rubrics_metrics.description: For biquadratic equations the radius of the circle used in Descartes' construction must be altered: its square is to be augmented or diminished by the rectangle formed by the latus rectum and the quantity r, depending on sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If r occurs with a negative sign (— r) add the rectangle a·r to the square of the basic radius; if r is +r, subtract a·r. The text explains doing this geometrically (taking EO and adjusting its square) so intersections still give correct roots; the same adjustment is absent when r is wanting (pure cubic case). Follow the algebra-to-geometry correspondences shown in the worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce cubic equations to biquadratics (multiply by z or use z±b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cubic equations should be transformed into biquadratic form before applying the general parabola+circle construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One approach shown is to multiply the cubic equation by z, producing a biquadratic 'wanting the last term r', then remove the second term and apply the construction. Another Schooten-derived approach multiplies by (z±b) when b is a term in the cubic, thereby producing a biquadratic with a known linear factor; the known root gives a point on the circumference and thus determines the circle. Worked examples demonstrate both techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the central-rule geometric investigations as an expedient preferred method
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric 'central rule' is presented as an especially expeditious and less caution-loaded way to determine the centre of the requisite circle for constructions, and is recommended over more intricate earlier rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction locates a point E on the axis (or a related parallel), erects perpendiculars, and takes prescribed segments (e.g., BK = 1/2 a, CE = ± p/2, FG = ± q/2 depending on signs) to find the centre G; GD (or similar) is the radius. The text argues this method is easier and avoids the many cautions of Baker and Schooten; follow the explicit compass-and-straightedge steps and refer to figures for implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If certain terms are missing, omit corresponding geometric elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When the 3rd or 4th term (p or q) or both are wanting in the equation, the corresponding parts of the geometric construction (lines CD, DE, etc.) derived from those quantities are omitted and the method proceeds with the remaining coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes no essential difference arises when terms are absent: simply leave out the segments deduced from missing coëfficients and continue with the rest of the construction per the examples. Several special-case examples are provided to show this simplification in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control variables strictly in comparative experiments (vacuum vs open air)
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing the effect of vacuum vs open air (e.g., dissolution in aquafortis, distillation), ensure equal pieces/quantities and identical heating so that observed differences may be attributed to the presence or absence of air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative experiment: two equal pieces of iron placed at the same time into equal quantities of aquafortis, one in vacuo and the other in open air; both taken out simultaneously and compared — the iron in open air was found 16 times more dissolved. For distillations, equal instrument design and identical heating are used. The text uses these controlled comparisons to justify causal claims about the role of air/vacuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and interpret unexpected phenomena in vacuum experiments (e.g., congealing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be attentive to qualitative differences produced by vacuum conditions (not only rates or yields) such as phase changes or congealing which may indicate different physical/chemical behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: rose-water distilled in vacuo 'did congeal', which does not occur in ordinary distillations — a datum used to argue vacuum affects distillation outcomes. Experimental reports should note such qualitative effects and consider when vacuum or compression may be advantageous depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess magnetic-variation observations for long-term, global reliability and local artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover any regular motion of the magnetic-needle's variation one needs exact observations made over the whole earth and at considerable time intervals; short, local, or inconsistent observations (e.g., pilot reports) are unreliable due to local iron and gross errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place too much reliance on pilots' observations because nearby iron (e.g., on a ship) can draw the needle and create spurious apparent variation; existing observations (only about 100 years and in limited places) cannot yet establish periodicity. The author therefore seeks methods 'independent of observations' to discover variation at sea. Design data collection campaigns that sample many locations and long durations and control for local ferrous interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making navigational inferences from compass readings taken near local iron sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that iron near the compass (for example on a ship) alters the needle's indication, producing apparent variation that may not reflect true geomagnetic variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recording magnetic variation for navigation or science, ensure the compass is situated away from iron and other magnetic disturbances; note and correct for local influences when comparing readings across time or place. The text uses this as a reason to distrust some sea observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate digester/engine improvements by measured efficiency metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess improvements to digesters and pneumatic/distillation engines by concrete performance measures: capacity, throughput, fuel consumption, and suitability for particular substances (stewed in own juices vs boiled with water).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example metrics from the review: a small engine holding 6–7 pounds of water will make 150 pounds of jelly in 24 hours consuming about 11 pounds of charcoal; alternative engine designs are proposed for items boiled in water (pulse, jellies) and for distilling by descensum with controlled rarefaction/condensation of air. Use such quantitative performance data when judging claimed 'improvements'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple qualitative tests to characterise biological fluids in autopsy
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply basic physical tests (e.g., boiling a serous fluid to observe thickening) to infer composition (nutritive juice vs urine etc.) during anatomical investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the serous liquor found in bladder vesiculae, when boiled, thickened into a stiff, glutinous jelly — a datum used to conjecture the liquor was 'nutritious juice' rather than ordinary urine. Record such simple diagnostic tests and report their outcomes alongside anatomical description.
